examples: You can also open this project up to encompass other mercreatures, such as merdogs, mercats, or merdeer.

senses: Perfect, excellent, brilliant.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish perfecto (“perfect”), from Latin perfectus. Doublet of parfait, perfect, and perfectus.

The act of grasping or gripping, especially with the hands.

ety: Borrowed from Latin prehensio, prehensionis. Doublet of prison.

A type of dough, originating in Mediterranean cuisine, that is used in thin layers to make pastries (such as baklava and apple strudel) and pies and becomes very flaky when cooked.
ety: From Greek φύλλο (fýllo, “leaf”). Doublet of phyllon, distantly also with foil, folio, and folium.

The classical system of yoga described in the Yoga Sutras by Patanjali.

ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit अष्टाङ्ग (aṣṭāṅga, “having eight parts”, literally “eight limbs”).

A wicker basket.
A unit of capacity with various specific local values.
A handbasket with two lids.
ety: From Middle English maunde, maundie, borrowed from Old French mande, borrowed from Middle Dutch mande, from Old Dutch *manda, from Proto-West Germanic *mandu.

senses: The (male) winner of a prize
Curved or bulged outward.
ety: From Middle English gibbous, from Latin gibbus (“humped, hunched”), probably cognate with cubō (“bend oneself, lie down”), Italian gobba (“humpback”), Ancient Greek κῡφός (kūphós, “humpback, bent”), κύβος (kúbos, “cube, vertebra”), Spanish giboso (“humped”). Also ultimately compare dialectal Norwegian keiv (“slanted, wrong”), German schief (“crooked, slanting”) and Dutch scheef (“crooked, slanting”).

senses: Enablement; giving the capacity to do something.
The process or act of stigmatizing.
examples: The Kaohsiung incident demonstrates how stigmatization can lead to real-world harm. CGM members in Taiwan have reported increased hostility in recent years, ranging from verbal harassment to institutional discrimination.

senses: A flavoring or fragrance used in foodstuffs and perfumes, derived from the tonka bean which contains coumarin.
ety: Likely from Guyanese Creole English tonka, from a Tupian language, perhaps Kari'na tonka.
examples: When grated into desserts or infused into syrups, they impart a flavour so transcendent, tonka has been dubbed the most delicious ingredient you’ve never heard of.
Her favourite combinations involve pine, boletus mushroom and sake, or celery, tonka and amber ale.
The word tonka is taken from the Galibi (Carib) tongue spoken by natives of French Guayana; it also appears in Tupi, another language of the same region, as the name of the tree.

senses: Characterized by giving love and affection.
Showing a decline of mental faculties, especially when it occurs in old age.
ety: From Middle English dotynge; equivalent to dote + -ing.

examples: The second Adigar is only entitled to twenty-four spearmen and fifteen whipcrackers.
He spoke : the brawny spearman let his cheek Bulge with the unswallow'd piece, and turning stared;
All around here the spearmen would hide, armed with those terrible shovel-balded spears that will kill a bullock at seventy yards.

senses: A person who makes manual copies of works such as manuscripts or paintings.
A giant vine native to South America (especially Banisteriopsis caapi), noted for its psychotropic properties.
ety: From Spanish ayahuasca, from Quechua ayawaska, from aya (“spirit, ancestor”) + waska (“vine”). First use appears c. 1870. See cite below.

senses: The bone at the center of a ham
examples: Perhaps I was afraid of being laughed at if the mysterious item turned out to be a hambone, a distinct possibility.

The bark of these plants, which yield quinine and other alkaloids useful in reducing fevers and particularly in combatting malaria.
ety: From New Latin cinchona, from Spanish Chinchón. Named by Carl Linnaeus after Ana de Osorio, 4th Countess of Chinchón (1599–1625), the wife of the Spanish Viceroy of Peru, who was allegedly cured of a fever by the bark.

senses: Disposed to litigate; contending in law; engaged in a lawsuit.
